name: ATtiny85 (PDIP-8)
summary: 8 KB AVR in an 8-pin package with five usable I/O. Every pin does three or four jobs, so the whole design problem is deciding what each one gives up.
notes: Arduino-style numbering under ATTinyCore / Digispark is PB0-PB5 = D0-D5, which is not the physical pin order. ADC channels are different again: ADC0 is on PB5, ADC1 on PB2, ADC2 on PB4, ADC3 on PB3.

PB5 is RESET by default, so you get four free I/O until you burn the RSTDISBL fuse. Doing that gives you a fifth pin but locks out ISP programming. After that you need a high-voltage programmer to recover the chip.
No hardware SPI or I2C. The USI block does the clocking, and the Arduino libraries (TinyWireM, USIWire) are built on it.
There is no hardware UART. Serial on an ATtiny85 is bit-banged software serial.
The USB bootloader boards (Digispark, micronucleus) take PB3 and PB4 for D- and D+, leaving PB0, PB1 and PB2.
Default fuses give 8 MHz internal with CKDIV8, so a fresh chip runs at 1 MHz. 16.5 MHz from the internal PLL is available and is what USB bootloaders use.
The speed grade tracks the supply, as on the ATmega328P: 20 MHz needs 4.5 V, 10 MHz needs 2.7 V.

pins.name: PB5
pins.note: Reset by default; needs a 10k pull-up. Usable as I/O only after disabling reset by fuse.

pins.name: PB1
pins.note: The LED pin on most ATtiny85 dev boards.

pins.name: PB2
pins.note: The only pin with a true external interrupt.

circuit.title: Minimum circuit to run

parts.why: Needed unless you have burned the RSTDISBL fuse, which is a one-way trip without a high-voltage programmer.

circuit.note: No crystal needed. The internal oscillator covers 1, 8 and 16.5 MHz, and the USB bootloader boards rely on it.
